Anyone using the dual-writer duration/error metrics to debug unified storage outages sees legacy-storage error counts increment for storage failures, pointing operators at the wrong backend during incidents.
records.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go` within `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the storage failure path records the wrong metric: after `res, async, err := d.Storage.Update(...)`, on `if err != nil { ... }` it calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure occurred in `d.Storage.Update`. This matches the finding that unified-store update failures would be attributed to legacy metrics.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The legacy write goroutines in Create/Update share the caller's `obj` (and objInfo/options in Update) with the synchronous storage write and the returned object without any synchronization, and return to the caller immediately. This is a data race under `go test -race` and in production: the API caller or Storage.Create mutates the object after Create returns while the goroutine still reads it; the race detector in CI will flake, and real concurrent mutation can send a torn or already-modified object to legacy storage, breaking dual-write consistency guarantees.
records.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Create`, after the synchronous `d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` the code immediately spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` using the same `obj` pointer (`go func() { ... _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...) ... }()`) with no cloning or synchronization, and returns to the caller right away. Similarly in `Update`, it spawns a goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ..., options)` reusing the same `objInfo` and `options` values that were passed to/used by the synchronous storage write. This matches the finding’s mechanism: shar

Operators running mode 3 during a legacy-storage outage get silent divergence between unified and legacy stores with no reconciliation hook, and tests (and downstream consumers like the playlist integration tests) that read legacy storage immediately after a create can observe the object missing — the new file/etcd mode-3 integration tests in this diff will flake on this timing window.

Every legacy write on a fast or slow request path races the request-context cancellation; when the request completes first the legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection is aborted mid-flight, so Mode 3 silently stops dual-writing and the two stores diverge with no error surfaced to the caller or the logs — the exact consistency guarantee Mode 3 exists to provide is dropped.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] All legacy writes (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) are spawned as unbounded, unordered, best-effort goroutines with no retry, no queue, no dedup, and no error logging, so under load operations reach legacy out of order or not at all. An Update immediately followed by a Delete on the same object can be applied to legacy in reverse order, leaving a deleted object permanently present in legacy storage; a single dropped goroutine (process restart, 10s timeout) leaves an unrecoverable divergence with no reconciliation path, and burst traffic spawns one goroutine per write with no backpressure against the legacy backend.
records.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, Mode3’s legacy writes were changed from inline best-effort to fire-and-forget goroutines. E.g. `Create` now does `go func() { ... _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...) ... }()` and immediately `return created, err` after the unified-store create succeeds. Similarly `Delete`, `Update`, and `DeleteCollection` kick off legacy operations in goroutines with `context.WithTimeoutCause(...)`. This makes legacy write failures unobservable by the caller and introduces a timing window where legacy storage may not reflect the write right after the API returns,

records.issue_text: [BUG] Create now performs the legacy-storage write in a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 10s timeout instead of the previous synchronous write, silently discarding legacy write failures and timed-out writes. When the legacy (SQL) store is slow or returns an error, the object exists only in unified storage; the dual-write contract that mode 3 keeps both stores consistent is broken with no error surfaced, and a legacy timeout silently abandons a write the caller believes was dual-written. No retry, no requeue, no metric on the dropped write beyond a latency label.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The DeleteCollection goroutine records its legacy-store call with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...), so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to storage. Legacy DeleteCollection failures (which indicate divergent undeleted rows in legacy) are recorded as storage successes/failures, hiding the exact divergence signal this metric exists to surface.
records.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go` within `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the storage failure path records the wrong metric: after `res, async, err := d.Storage.Update(...)`, on `if err != nil { ... }` it calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure occurred in `d.Storage.Update`. This matches the finding that unified-store update failures would be attributed to legacy metrics.

records.issue_text: [BUG] Create's legacy write is a fire-and-forget goroutine whose error is only recorded as a metric — no log, no retry, no surfaced failure. When d.Legacy.Create fails (or times out after 10s), the API returns success and the legacy store permanently diverges from unified storage with zero log line; operators discover it only via a metrics dashboard, and rollback to legacy storage serves stale/missing objects.
records.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, Mode3’s legacy writes were changed from inline best-effort to fire-and-forget goroutines. E.g. `Create` now does `go func() { ... _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...) ... }()` and immediately `return created, err` after the unified-store create succeeds. Similarly `Delete`, `Update`, and `DeleteCollection` kick off legacy operations in goroutines with `context.WithTimeoutCause(...)`. This makes legacy write failures unobservable by the caller and introduces a timing window where legacy storage may not reflect the write right after the API returns,

records.issue_text: [BUG] The async legacy goroutines derive their context from the request-scoped ctx, which is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns. Because the API responds immediately after the unified-store write and the goroutine runs after the handler completes, the apiserver cancels the request context before the legacy write finishes, so legacy writes routinely abort with context.Canceled — the dual write effectively never happens for slow legacy stores.

records.issue_text: [BUG] Update no longer uses updateWrapper, so the legacy write re-computes UpdatedObject from objInfo against legacy storage's own old state instead of persisting the object the unified store already accepted. If objInfo's transformation is not idempotent (e.g. timestamp regeneration, RV-derived defaults) or legacy's old object differs, legacy stores a different object version than unified storage — the exact skew updateWrapper existed to prevent — while both writes still 'succeed'.
